1.pericope_label: The law of the sin offering introduced

schools.summary: Gill hears in the opening formula either a continuation or a fresh start after some pause, and notes that the law, like the rest, bound Israel and such as were proselyted to them. Calvin explains why the sin offering comes first in importance: without reconciliation there is no intercourse between men and God, who deservedly abominates the race for the corruption of our nature, so the whole hope of salvation rests on the remedies provided for propitiating him. He also notes that a distinction is laid down between persons, one victim being required of a king, another of the priests, another of ordinary men, with regard had to the poor that they be not burdened as the rich are; and he narrows the ignorance meant, denying that all kinds are included and taking the Hebrew for a sin into which a perplexed mind has been driven by some passion, through thoughtlessness or imprudence.

Henry treats the opening words as a seam, the laws of the first three chapters seeming delivered at one time while here begin the statutes of another day, spoken from the throne of glory between the cherubim. What follows he calls more strictly new than anything before: burnt, meat and peace offerings had been made before Sinai, but the law being added because of transgressions, men were put into a way of atoning more particularly by sacrifice, which more than any other ceremonial institution was a shadow of good things to come, the substance being Christ. He also sets the boundary on the other side, that sin is the transgression of the divine law and the wits or wills of men cannot make that a sin which God's law has not made one.

Clarke lists the chapter's divisions and draws the sharpest practical consequence, that a man's ignorance is no excuse: as soon as the transgression comes to his knowledge he must bring the sacrifice, and if he refuses he sins obstinately and wilfully, so that nothing remains for him but a fearful looking for of judgment, which Clarke takes to be the case the apostle has in view. Wesley argues the limit from practicality, since if every daily infirmity had required an offering most sinners could not have borne the charge, nor the altar received so many, nor the priests managed so infinite a work; he asks too why negative commands are singled out, and answers that affirmative precepts do not bind men so strictly and constantly.

Ellicott reaches Henry's conclusion from the grammar, since the earlier offerings are spoken of in the voluntary formula if any man of you bring, while here the words are if a soul shall sin, let him bring, the sin offering entering as a new injunction; he gives the plain sense of ignorance as acting inadvertently and recognising the fault afterwards, and adds the four conditions the second Temple attached to it. Keil and Delitzsch set out the four classes of offerer and observe that the ritual differed for each in the animal, the sprinkling of the blood and the treatment of the flesh, according to the offerer's position in the kingdom of God.

themes: if a soul shall sin through ignorance
the sin offering as a new institution
the ritual graded by the offerer’s rank
is ignorance an excuse?

3.pericope_label: The sin offering for the anointed priest

schools.summary: Gill notes that the Targums and the Greek read the anointed priest for the high priest, and draws the apostle's inference, that the law made men high priests who had infirmity and needed to offer for themselves as well as for others, by which it appeared perfection could not be had under that priesthood. He observes that the priest took the blood himself and not by deputy, being his own suppliant, and that the sprinkling went by the right hand, the rabbinic canons counting the left invalid. Calvin turns rank into obligation, the more illustrious the dignity the more closely the life should be conformed to holiness, so that a failing tolerable in others grew reprehensible in him; and he meets the awkwardness of a guilty man performing the office of reconciliation by answering that the law of the priesthood was inviolable and no further mediators could lawfully be appointed, so God stretched his grace over the fault rather than let men look elsewhere for pardon.

Clarke reports critics who render the clause if the anointed priest shall lead the people to sin, glossing it as the shepherd straying and the flock following, and sets out the three applications of the blood, sprinkled seven times before the veil, smeared on the horns of the incense altar, and the residue poured at the foot of the brazen one. Wesley notes that the man was not complete in the dignity until anointed, gives both readings of the disputed clause and treats the second as an aggravation, since such a fall commonly brings guilt and punishment on men scandalised by it; he also observes that entry into the tabernacle with the blood was neither required nor allowed on any other occasion, possibly to mark how grave the offence was.

Ellicott argues that by adducing the chief of the order as the first instance, the law shows him a frail being exposed to the same infirmities as the laity, and so forestalls any claim of spiritual superiority; he adds that the title the priest that is anointed belongs to this book alone, where it occurs four times, the rest of the Pentateuch and Joshua saying the great priest, and marks the movement of the blood indoors from the court where the beast was killed into the tent of meeting. Keil and Delitzsch explain the title from the completeness of the unction consecrating him to office, refer the disputed clause to his official standing as the nation's representative before God rather than to his private relation to him, and note that the ox is the largest beast on the list, the offerer filling the highest post in Israel.

debates.question: What does “according to the sin of the people” mean?

sides.position: a comparison — he sinned as any layman might, though more circumspection was expected of him
a consequence — he sinned so as to lead the people into sin, the shepherd straying and the flock following
an official capacity — he sinned as the nation’s representative before God, not merely as a private man

themes: if the priest that is anointed do sin
according to the sin of the people
the blood carried into the tent of meeting
why the greatest victim for the greatest office

13.pericope_label: The sin offering for the whole congregation

schools.summary: Gill begins with all Israel or the bulk of them, misled by the ignorant teaching of judges whose instruction makes the nation err, but reports that Jarchi and others understand the sanhedrim, the bench of seventy-one; he quotes Ainsworth's terse comment that the church may err, and collects the range of opinion on how many elders laid on hands, two at least, some saying three and some five, with three of the sanhedrim the more generally received view, though the Targum of Jonathan makes them the twelve rulers of the twelve tribes. Calvin approaches the case through the phrase if the thing be hid, allowing that it covers the infirmity of men blinded for a season who do not search themselves and so slumber, and holding that a whole people may miss its own sin while dealing with itself too gently; the point of the law is that once awakened to acknowledge the fault they must still propitiate God, or they would make their error a cloak. He explains the equal victim by the fact that the man who entered the sanctuary in the name of all stood for the whole body.

Henry makes this the law for expiating a national guilt, supposing that leaders may mistake the law and lead their people astray, the offering being brought once the error is found so that wrath may not fall on all. God will always have a church on earth, he says, but he never promised it should be infallible or perfectly pure from corruption this side of heaven. The offence he imagines is a common usage taken up on the presumption that it was lawful, which upon later search proved otherwise, and neither the commonness of the practice nor the general opinion of its lawfulness excuses the people from bringing an atonement; he has the elders act as representatives and agents of the people, three at the least.

Clarke supposes some oversight in worship or transgression of the letter of the law arising from peculiar circumstances, and instances the men who after the long fight with the Philistines flew on the spoil and ate with the blood, which he connects with Saul's rash adjuration; he follows Maimonides for three of the Sanhedrin laying on hands in the name of all. Wesley takes the congregation for the body of the people or the greater part, their rulers concurring, and adds from Numbers that where the fault was merely the omission of a ceremonial duty a kid of the goats sufficed.

Ellicott sets both readings of congregation side by side, the plain construction making the two words one body used interchangeably, so that those who inadvertently offended are those who afterwards recognised the fault, and the interpretation current in the time of Christ making them the great Sanhedrin, representatives who might through error proclaim a mistaken decree. He notes the animal is the same as for the anointed priest and must be without blemish though the text does not repeat it, and disposes of a misreading of the phrase about bringing the bullock before the tent of meeting, which is the ordinary Hebrew idiom for causing a thing to be brought and no more means that the thousands of Israel each carry it than the earlier wording means the high priest carried his own.

debates.question: Who is “the whole congregation of Israel”?

sides.position: the body of the people, or the greater part, their rulers concurring
the great Sanhedrin, the representatives who might proclaim a mistaken decree — the interpretation current in the time of Christ

the church may err

20.pericope_label: The sin offering for a ruler

schools.summary: Gill derives the Hebrew from a root meaning to lift up or bear, so the man is one raised above others or one carrying the weight of government, and reports Aben Ezra allowing the head of a household or tribe, the Talmud making it a tribal prince, and Maimonides and Gersom holding that a king is meant; on the discovery of the fault he allows either that others informed him or that he called his own act to mind and weighed it against the law. Calvin cuts the knot by observing that no law had yet made one man ruler, so Moses must mean heads and governors generally, named because men in authority do more harm by a bad example than private persons can; and he reads the scale of the offerings as designed so that men in office should keep the more carefully from every transgression, whereas they are otherwise apt to indulge themselves, as though rank allowed a wider licence.

Henry seizes the possessive in the commandment of the Lord his God and makes it the lesson: God takes notice of the sins of rulers, and those who have power to call others to account are themselves accountable to the ruler of rulers, for high as they are there is a higher than they; he is a prince to other men, but let him know that the Lord is a God to him. Henry also makes the moment of discovery a duty, since it comes by the check of conscience or the reproof of friends, both of which even the best of us should not merely submit to but be thankful for, and turns it into a daily petition that God would teach what we do not see; and he marks the three ways the ritual falls short of the earlier, a kid rather than a bullock, no blood carried into the tabernacle, and the whole of it bestowed on the brazen altar.

Clarke thinks any political dignity may be covered, granting that the rabbins read it of the king, and notes that the rites are nearly as before except that the fat was burnt as in the peace offering. Wesley notes only that the bullock called the first here is the one brought for the priest's own sin.

Ellicott admits the word carries all three senses and then argues from a detail nobody else notices, that in the other cases the fault is simply against any commandment of the Lord whereas here alone the text says of the Lord his God, from which the second Temple drew its reading that the man is one over whom God alone is exalted; he also corrects the closing clause, which is not and is guilty but and acknowledges his guilt. Keil and Delitzsch take the word for the head of a tribe or tribal division, suppose someone drew the ruler's attention to his transgression, and give the sequence of the rite in full, adding that the buck-goat is named again and again for a sin offering.

debates.question: Who is the “ruler” of this law?

sides.position: a king, over whom none has power — the reading the second Temple drew from the phrase “his God”
the head of a tribe or of a tribal division
any political dignity whatever, or heads and governors generally, no law having yet made one man ruler

the commandment of the Lord his God
and acknowledges his guilt
a kid of the goats, a male without blemish

27.pericope_label: The sin offering for one of the common people

schools.summary: Gill renders the Hebrew one soul of the people of the earth, a single man distinguished from the congregation and neither high priest nor prince nor king but a common priest or Levite or lay Israelite, and takes occasion to say that no man is free from sin, all ranks and degrees sinning continually either ignorantly or willingly, and that Christ is a sacrifice for all sins and for every sort of sinner.

Henry lays the two laws side by side and finds only two differences, that a private man might bring either a kid or a lamb where the ruler was confined to a kid, and that the ruler's beast had to be male where the commoner's was female. What he draws from the case is that the meanest are as much within the law as the greatest: Jeremiah supposes the poor not so likely as the great men to know the way of the Lord, and yet if they sin through ignorance they must bring an offering, since even sins of ignorance need atoning for by sacrifice. To plead that we did it ignorantly and under the surprise of temptation will not bring us off, he says, unless we have an interest in that greater plea, that Christ has died; and he turns it into David's prayer, himself a ruler, to be cleansed from secret faults, the errors a man does not understand in himself.

Clarke translates the phrase people of the land and thinks it may reach the very lowest, the labouring or agricultural classes; he takes the close of the chapter as the place to recapitulate, stating the whole procedure in one sequence — the victim brought to the door of the tabernacle, the hands laid on its head, the sacrifice acknowledged as the offerer's own and needed for his offence, the sin thereby confessed and reckoned as transferred to the animal, and the blood then spilt to make the atonement — and refuses to let the institution rest there, since such ordinances could not be considered as terminating in themselves. Wesley gives the reason for the lesser victim, that the sin of such a person was less than the sin of a ruler.

Ellicott defines the offerer by exclusion, any member of the congregation who is neither the anointed priest nor the ruler already named, repeats his correction that the closing words mean not and is guilty but and acknowledges his guilt, and notes that the Hebrew word is feminine, a she-goat being of smaller value and so suited to the means of ordinary people. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the mechanics, tracing the same order as for the ruler down to the burning of the fat for a sweet savour, whereupon the priest makes atonement and it is forgiven him.

themes: if any one of the common people sin
even sins of ignorance need atonement
cleanse thou me from secret faults
the sin transferred to the victim

32.pericope_label: The lamb brought instead of the goat

schools.summary: Gill reports the Jewish writers' observation that a lamb is elsewhere always named before a goat as the more excellent of the two in its kind, and their inference from its standing after the goat here that the two are held equally alike; he notes that the hand is laid on the head of the lamb as on the head of the goat, and, following the Targum, that it is the right hand.

Wesley observes that the command to burn them uses a plural because the fat was of several kinds, and that the Hebrew reads upon the offerings made by fire, meaning together with them or after them, since the burnt offerings were to have the first place.

Ellicott renders the word sheep rather than lamb and takes the provision as a concession to means, those unable to bring a goat offering a female sheep as the less valuable animal provided it was without blemish; he explains that the sheep is given a paragraph of its own though the ritual is identical because the fat tail had to be burned with the rest. He makes the same correction as Wesley about the fire, explaining that the daily morning sacrifice lay burning on the altar all the forenoon so that no fresh fire was kindled for what followed, and closes on a distinction running back through the chapter, that the flesh of the sin offering for a ruler and for a private Israelite fell to the priests and was eaten by them rather than being burnt outside the camp, which is consistent with the rule that the sinner who brought the offering could not partake of it — so the priest might not eat of what he offered for his own sin, nor of the congregation's, being himself a member of it.

debates.question: Is the sheep a lesser alternative to the goat?

sides.position: yes; it is the less valuable animal, offered by those unable to bring a goat
no; the Jewish writers infer from its position here that lamb and goat are held equally alike
